finding.claim: The nightly sync() issues a server-side GET to iconUrl, which is set from the unvalidated `icon` parameter of update(), so an attacker can make the server request arbitrary URLs (internal hosts, localhost, cloud metadata endpoints). The response is discarded, so this is blind SSRF.
finding.source: `icon` parameter of Profile.update(String webhook, String icon) (src/Profile.java:11), reachable from PUT /profile per the comment at line 10.
finding.sink: c.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(URI.create(iconUrl)).GET().build(), ...) at src/Profile.java:23-24, run by sync() at line 20.

trace.note: Entry point: PUT /profile, attacker-supplied request body.
this.iconUrl = icon; stored with no validation.
Comment: sync() is a nightly job, so the fetch runs server-side later.
URI.create(iconUrl) parses the stored value with no scheme, host, or address check; GET is sent.

finding.guards_checked: update() at lines 12-14 validates only `webhook` against https://hooks\.example\.com/[A-Za-z0-9]{20}. `icon` has no validation: no scheme allowlist, host allowlist, private/loopback/link-local IP blocking, or port restriction. No redirect handling is visible in this file. The HttpClient is injected by the caller at line 20, so its redirect policy and proxy settings can't be checked here; the JDK default is to not follow redirects. Only one sink exists for the icon URL, and iconUrl is written only in update(). Exploitability depends on network position of the job (cloud metadata, internal services). Severity assessment is left to the reviewer.

verdict.guard_found: none. Profile.java:12 validates only `webhook` (regex on hooks.example.com); `icon` is assigned unchecked at line 16 and passed straight to URI.create at line 23. No scheme, host, private-IP, or port check exists anywhere in the file.
verdict.reason: Attacker-supplied `icon` from the PUT /profile update() (Profile.java:11) is stored unvalidated at line 16 and used as the GET target at lines 23-24 in sync() (line 20), so the server issues a request to an arbitrary URL. The file confirms the trace; the PUT /profile routing is taken from the comment at line 10 since no route handler is in the code available to me, and the redirect/proxy policy of the injected HttpClient is not visible here, which affects severity but not the verdict.

finding.claim: Not a finding: the webhook URL fetched by sync() is validated.

trace.note: String.matches() requires a full-string match against https://hooks\.example\.com/[A-Za-z0-9]{20}.
Only validated value is stored in webhookUrl.

finding.guards_checked: The anchored regex fixes scheme, host, and path. The path segment admits only alphanumerics, so userinfo (@), fragment (#), query (?), and extra path segments are rejected. Host is fixed to hooks.example.com. No redirect or DNS-rebinding bypass is visible given the fixed host, so this sink is not reported.

verdict.guard_found: src/Profile.java:12 is a full-string anchored match (String.matches) on https://hooks\.example\.com/[A-Za-z0-9]{20}. It fixes scheme and host, and the character class rejects @, #, ?, and extra path segments. Only the validated value is stored at line 15 and used at lines 21-22.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: the `webhook` parameter at src/Profile.java:11 is attacker-reachable via PUT /profile, but the anchored full-string regex at src/Profile.java:12 pins the host to hooks.example.com before the value is stored at line 15 and passed to URI.create at line 21, which is a closing guard. The one residual caveat is that redirect behavior depends on the caller-supplied HttpClient, which the code does not show.
